Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-polish-long-0051", "row_sha256": "f465b6d2ec1e779e2c5cf5d8b2bf2a4601f6c018a7d7d13124c862ce4b2aa7d9", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {"profile": "Clear and professional."}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
our lighting crew at the bellwether room is small, four people when everyone is available, and the room itself is a converted upstairs hall with a low grid and a narrow loading stair. mara is the production electrician, jo runs the board, and ellis and i handle fixtures and cable; i am usually the person who keeps the paper notes, though jo sometimes takes that job when i am on the ladder. we do not have a separate storage room, so the road cases live behind the black traveler until a visiting company needs that corner. the arrangement is workable, but moving a case through the room can become a little awkward once the audience chairs are set.

this spring we are preparing a revival of the play the glass orchard, which uses twelve conventional fixtures, six led units, two practical lamps and a small haze machine. the director, lena vale, wants the kitchen to feel warm without making the orchard scenes look orange. jo described the early palette as “a little honeyed, but not syrupy,” and we have been using that phrase when we compare the rehearsal looks. the script has three scene changes that happen in near darkness, and the cast cross the upstage platform during two of them. because the platform edge is only marked with low glow tape, the first rehearsal showed that a bright side special could make the tape disappear from the actors’ view. we lowered that special and noted the change on the plot, although the final level is still a choice for the next cue-to-cue.

our hang schedule has to fit around the acting company, who rehearse in the hall most afternoons. we can get ladders into the room on monday and wednesday mornings, and the building manager has asked us not to leave anything across the east fire door overnight. mara wants all overhead fixtures hung and safety-checked before the first focus session; that is a firm part of the plan, not a preference. if the dimmer rack has not been powered for at least twenty minutes before jo checks the led addresses, we will postpone that address check rather than rush it. the rack has behaved normally so far, but its display takes a while to settle after a cold start. we have told the stage manager, dev, that the schedule may shift by half an hour if that condition comes up.

1. before the first ladder goes up, ellis checks each cable for a damaged jacket and puts any questionable lead on the marked shelf by the booth. he writes the fixture number on a strip of masking tape, but the tape is only a temporary label and not a substitute for the proper color code. i enter the fixture number and its position into the paper plot, then jo checks that the channel assignment is the same in the console file. in the last room we worked, we found one lead with a split near the connector, so we are perhaps slightly more cautious about inspecting the ends than we were at the start of the season. the damaged lead is not part of this production’s inventory, and nobody has suggested using it.

2. focus is done with the actors out of the room where possible, because a quiet hall makes it easier to hear the spotter and keeps people clear of the ladders. mara calls the shutter and tilt adjustments; the person at the desk changes the channel only after she confirms the fixture number. on tuesday, jo thought a lantern was aimed at the orchard bench, but it was actually the neighboring unit, which had a similar angle from the floor. we stopped, read both labels, and corrected the plot before carrying on. it did not alter the cue order, though it took longer than we had allowed. the director watched the last part of that focus and said, “I can see the leaves now, but I still want the table to be the first thing you notice.” we have not yet decided whether that means a lower level on the leaf break-up or a small change to the table special.

3. the practical lamps are supplied by the props department, not our crew, and they need to be in their final positions before we finish the stage-right circuits. if props changes the lamp positions after that point, we will recheck the cable path and the shadows on the wall before the next run. this condition matters because one lamp sits close to the legs of the upstage platform, where a loose cable could be hard to see during a dark change. dev has asked props to keep the plug end facing the wall, although we have not yet seen the lamps set in place. until they are there, we can test the outlet and leave the circuit labelled, but we cannot confirm the final look of the practicals. our notes say that plainly so nobody mistakes an empty rehearsal position for a completed focus.

we are keeping the paperwork simple because there is no production electrician assigned for the second week of performances. the current plot has a page for each area, a separate list of borrowed equipment, and a cue sheet with the rehearsal names rather than just the cue numbers. that makes it easier for the person covering jo to follow the conversation at the desk. the borrowed equipment list includes two floor pockets from the studio next door and a short length of black border; the studio manager wants both returned by the friday after closing. mara has put the return date on the outside of the case, and i have also written it in the notebook. this is perhaps more reminder than we need, but borrowed items have gone missing between rooms before, and the studio is using those pockets the following week.

at the end of each work session, ellis coils the spare cable, jo saves the console file under the date and rehearsal name, and i photograph any plot changes that are not yet transferred to the clean copy. we leave the work lights on for the building staff and switch off the practical tests at the wall, since those lamps are not on the lighting desk. if we have used haze, the stage manager opens the hall doors for a few minutes after the actors have left; the building manager asked us not to run the machine during the afternoon classes. we have not needed to use haze in rehearsal yet, so the cleanup note is there for later rather than a record of something already done.

on the next cue-to-cue, we will check the dark changes with the cast moving at their usual pace, then look at the platform edge from the front row and from the stage-right entrance. lena may ask for another adjustment to the orchard look, and i think that is likely, but the current notes do not show a new level yet. if the side special still makes the glow tape hard to see, we will lower it again or test a different angle before the cast repeat the crossing. we also need to confirm the practical lamps after props places them, and to check that the borrowed floor pockets are still clear of the route to the east fire door. until those checks happen, the focus record remains a working copy, with the open choices marked for the next session.", "output": "Our lighting crew at the Bellwether Room is small: four people when everyone is available. The room itself is a converted upstairs hall with a low grid and a narrow loading stair. Mara is the production electrician, Jo runs the board, and Ellis and I handle fixtures and cable. I am usually the person who keeps the paper notes, though Jo sometimes takes that job when I am on the ladder. We do not have a separate storage room, so the road cases live behind the black traveler until a visiting company needs that corner. The arrangement is workable, but moving a case through the room can become slightly awkward once the audience chairs are set.

This spring we are preparing a revival of the play The Glass Orchard, which uses twelve conventional fixtures, six LED units, two practical lamps, and a small haze machine. The director, Lena Vale, wants the kitchen to feel warm without making the orchard scenes look orange. Jo described the early palette as “a little honeyed, but not syrupy,” and we have been using that phrase when comparing the rehearsal looks. The script has three scene changes that happen in near darkness, and the cast crosses the upstage platform during two of them. Because the platform edge is marked only with low-glow tape, the first rehearsal showed that a bright side special could make the tape disappear from the actors’ view. We lowered that special and noted the change on the plot, although the final level remains a choice for the next cue-to-cue.

Our hang schedule has to fit around the acting company, which rehearses in the hall most afternoons. We can get ladders into the room on Monday and Wednesday mornings, and the building manager has asked us not to leave anything across the east fire door overnight. Mara wants all overhead fixtures hung and safety-checked before the first focus session; that is a firm part of the plan, not a preference. If the dimmer rack has not been powered for at least twenty minutes before Jo checks the LED addresses, we will postpone that address check rather than rush it. The rack has behaved normally so far, but its display takes a while to settle after a cold start. We have told the stage manager, Dev, that the schedule may shift by half an hour if that condition comes up.

1. Before the first ladder goes up, Ellis checks each cable for a damaged jacket and puts any questionable lead on the marked shelf by the booth. He writes the fixture number on a strip of masking tape, but the tape is only a temporary label, not a substitute for the proper color code. I enter the fixture number and its position in the paper plot, then Jo checks that the channel assignment matches the console file. In the last room we worked in, we found one lead with a split near the connector, so we are perhaps slightly more cautious about inspecting the ends than we were at the start of the season. The damaged lead is not part of this production’s inventory, and nobody has suggested using it.

2. We focus with the actors out of the room where possible, because a quiet hall makes it easier to hear the spotter and keeps people clear of the ladders. Mara calls the shutter and tilt adjustments; the person at the desk changes the channel only after she confirms the fixture number. On Tuesday, Jo thought a lantern was aimed at the orchard bench, but it was actually the neighboring unit, which looked as if it had a similar angle from the floor. We stopped, read both labels, and corrected the plot before continuing. This did not alter the cue order, though it took longer than we had allowed. The director watched the last part of that focus and said, “I can see the leaves now, but I still want the table to be the first thing you notice.” We have not yet decided whether that means a lower level on the leaf break-up or a small change to the table special.

3. The practical lamps are supplied by the props department, not our crew, and they need to be in their final positions before we finish the stage-right circuits. If props changes the lamp positions after that point, we will recheck the cable path and the shadows on the wall before the next run. This condition matters because one lamp sits close to the legs of the upstage platform, where a loose cable could be hard to see during a dark change. Dev has asked props to keep the plug end facing the wall, although we have not yet seen the lamps set in place. Until they are there, we can test the outlet and leave the circuit labeled, but we cannot confirm the practicals’ final look. Our notes state this plainly so nobody mistakes an empty rehearsal position for a completed focus.

We are keeping the paperwork simple because there is no production electrician assigned for the second week of performances. The current plot has a page for each area, a separate list of borrowed equipment, and a cue sheet with the rehearsal names rather than just the cue numbers. That makes it easier for the person covering Jo to follow the conversation at the desk. The borrowed equipment list includes two floor pockets from the studio next door and a short length of black border; the studio manager wants both returned by the Friday after closing. Mara has put the return date on the outside of the case, and I have also written it in the notebook. This is perhaps more of a reminder than we need, but borrowed items have gone missing between rooms before, and the studio is using those pockets the following week.

At the end of each work session, Ellis coils the spare cable, Jo saves the console file under the date and rehearsal name, and I photograph any plot changes that have not yet been transferred to the clean copy. We leave the work lights on for the building staff and switch off the practical tests at the wall, since those lamps are not on the lighting desk. If we have used haze, the stage manager opens the hall doors for a few minutes after the actors have left; the building manager asked us not to run the machine during the afternoon classes. We have not needed to use haze in rehearsal yet, so the cleanup note is there for later, rather than as a record of something already done.

At the next cue-to-cue, we will check the dark changes with the cast moving at their usual pace, then look at the platform edge from the front row and the stage-right entrance. Lena may ask for another adjustment to the orchard look, and I think that is likely, but the current notes do not show a new level yet. If the side special still makes the glow tape hard to see, we will lower it again or test a different angle before the cast repeat the crossing. We also need to confirm the practical lamps after props places them and check that the borrowed floor pockets are still clear of the route to the east fire door. Until those checks happen, the focus record remains a working copy, with the open choices marked for the next session."}]
